title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 31
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: Measuring the Candidate
passages.text:
A. The written examination was introduced as a reform, and understanding that is necessary to understanding everything that followed. The alternative it replaced was appointment by patronage, family connection and personal recommendation, and an anonymous written test administered to all comers was a device for taking selection out of the hands of people who knew the candidates. Its purpose was fairness, and its defenders were not the conservatives of their day.

B. What made it work also made it narrow. A test can only be marked consistently if the qualities it examines can be judged the same way by different markers, which excludes a great deal that matters and includes a great deal that can be scored. The examination measures what it can measure reliably, and the assumption that this coincides with what is worth knowing has never been demonstrated and is generally not examined.

C. The consequences for teaching were visible almost immediately and have been rediscovered in every generation since. Where a test carries serious consequences, instruction moves towards the test, and the closer the alignment the less the score reveals about anything beyond itself. A measure that is used to allocate opportunity stops measuring the thing it was designed to measure, which is a general property of measures rather than a failing of examinations in particular.

D. Objective formats were introduced to remove the marker's judgement and introduced problems of their own. Scoring became consistent and cheap, comparisons across large populations became possible, and the range of things that could be asked contracted sharply towards recognition and away from construction. The efficiency was real; the cost was that the format determined the content rather than the reverse.

E. Fairness claims require more care than they usually receive. A test administered identically to everyone is procedurally fair and can still produce results that track family income closely, because preparation is purchasable and familiarity with the format is itself a trained skill. Identical treatment of candidates who arrive with unequal preparation produces a defensible procedure and an outcome that reproduces the advantages it was created to bypass.

F. No serious alternative has displaced it, which is the fact that any criticism has to accommodate. Continuous assessment is vulnerable to unequal help at home; interviews reintroduce exactly the personal judgement examinations were built to remove; portfolios are difficult to compare. The examination survives not because it is good at what it claims but because the alternatives fail in ways that are worse and more familiar.

passages.title: The Ocean Leaning
passages.text:
Tides are caused by gravity, and almost every popular explanation of how gets the mechanism wrong. The moon does not simply pull the ocean towards it; if it did there would be one high tide a day rather than two. What matters is the difference in the moon's pull across the width of the Earth — stronger on the near side, weaker on the far side than on the planet's centre — and it is this difference, not the pull itself, that stretches the ocean into a bulge at both ends.

That two-bulge arrangement explains the basic rhythm and almost nothing about any actual coastline. As the Earth rotates beneath the bulges, most places pass through two highs and two lows a day, but the size and timing at any particular location depend on the shape of the sea floor, the width of the entrance to a bay, the length of the coastline and the natural period at which that body of water sloshes. The astronomical cause is uniform; the local result is not.

Resonance is why some places have enormous tides and their neighbours do not. A bay whose natural oscillation period is close to the tidal period amplifies the incoming tide much as a pushed swing gains height from small regular pushes, and ranges of many metres occur in a few such places while an open coastline nearby may see less than one. This is a property of the basin's geometry rather than of its position relative to the moon.

The sun contributes about half as much as the moon despite being far more massive, because the tidal effect depends on the difference in pull across the Earth rather than on the pull's total strength, and that difference falls very steeply with distance. When sun and moon align their effects add, producing the largest tides; when they are at right angles the effects partly cancel, producing the smallest. The fortnightly alternation follows directly.

The tides are also, slowly, changing the length of the day. Friction between the moving water and the sea floor dissipates energy, which acts as a brake on the Earth's rotation, and the angular momentum lost is transferred to the moon's orbit — so days lengthen very gradually and the moon recedes. Both effects are measurable with modern instruments and confirmed independently by growth patterns in ancient shells and corals.

Predicting tides was among the earliest successes of applied computation, and it succeeded for an unusual reason. The astronomical forcing is a sum of a manageable number of regular cycles, so once the response of a particular port has been measured for long enough, its future tides can be calculated indefinitely without understanding the fluid dynamics at all. It is a rare case where an empirical fit to a complicated system genuinely does the work that theory cannot.

passages.title: Thrown Away Before Anyone Eats
passages.text:
Roughly a third of the food produced for people is never eaten, and the figure is quoted far more often than it is disaggregated. What is lost, where it is lost and why differ so completely between rich and poor countries that a single global number obscures the two distinct problems it combines, and a solution appropriate to one is usually irrelevant to the other.

In lower-income countries most loss happens before the food reaches anyone. Crops are damaged during harvest, spoil in storage without refrigeration, or are destroyed in transit on poor roads, and the loss falls on producers who can least absorb it. These are engineering and infrastructure problems with known solutions — better storage, cold chains, roads — whose limitation is capital rather than knowledge.

In higher-income countries the loss is concentrated at the end of the chain, in retail and above all in households, and its causes are behavioural and economic rather than technical. Food is cheap relative to income, so the cost of discarding it is low; portions and package sizes are set for convenience rather than consumption; and date labelling is widely misread, with a substantial share of household disposal involving food that was still perfectly edible on the day it was thrown out.

Retail practices contribute in ways that are less visible than they appear in campaigns. Cosmetic specifications reject produce that is edible but misshapen, and the rejection happens at the field rather than the shop, so it never appears in retail waste statistics at all. Well-stocked shelves until closing time require a predictable surplus, and the surplus is the cost of the availability that customers demonstrably prefer.

The environmental case is stronger than the humanitarian one, which is the reverse of how it is usually argued. Wasted food does not reach hungry people even if it is saved, because the barrier is distribution and income rather than supply; what is unambiguous is that producing it consumed land, water, fuel and fertiliser to no purpose, and that its decomposition emits methane. On that accounting food waste is a large environmental cost independent of any nutritional argument.

Interventions divide sharply by whether they need anyone to change their mind. Clearer date labels, smaller default portions, storage guidance printed where it will be seen, and redistribution logistics work by changing what is easy rather than what is believed, and they show measurable results. Campaigns urging households to waste less perform poorly on their own, which by now is a familiar finding in every field where it has been tested.
